Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter checklist1
3B

Key ideas

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Definitions

Photon: a quantum of light or other electromagnetic radiation
Ionise: the removal or addition of electrons from a neutral atom
Alpha (α) particle: a radioactive decay product comprising two protons and two neutrons; the same as a He nucleus
Transmutation: a change in the structure of atomic nuclei that converts one element into another element
Beta (β) particle: a high-energy, high-speed electron (β−) or positron (β+) that is ejected from the nucleus by some radionuclides during a form of radioactive decay

Formulas

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, 3B glossary and formula boxes2
3B

Key ideas

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Definitions

Gamma (γ) ray: a high-energy photon released when a nucleus remains unstable after alpha or beta decay. Gamma rays travel at the speed of light and carry no charge.
Nuclear transformation: the conversion of one nuclide into another nuclide

Formulas

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, 3B glossary and formula boxes3
3B

New knowledgeDifferent types of radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Following the 1896 discovery of radioactivity by Henri Becquerel, Ernest Rutherford (Figure 3B–2 left) in 1899 studied the absorption of radioactivity by thin sheets of metal foil and found two components: alpha (represented by the symbol α) radiation, which is absorbed by a few thousandths of a centimetre of metal foil or a sheet of paper, and beta (represented by the symbol β) radiation, which can pass through 100 times as much foil before it was absorbed.

Shortly afterwards, a third form of radiation, named gamma (represented by the symbol γ) rays, were discovered that can penetrate as much as several centimetres of lead (Figure 3B–2 right).

Unstable isotopes emit various types of radiation as they transform to stable isotopes.

There are three naturally occurring forms of nuclear radiation: α-, β- and γ-radiation (Figure 3B–3).

Figure 3B–2 Only three years after the discovery of radioactivity, the physicist Ernest Rutherford (left) found that three different kinds of radiation are emitted in the decay of radioactive substances; these he called alpha, beta and gamma rays in sequence based on how far they could penetrate matter (right).
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 204
3B

New knowledgeDifferent types of radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

When these different types of radiation were first discovered, Ernest Rutherford did not know exactly what they were.

So each type of radiation was given a different Greek letter (in this case the first three letters of the Greek alphabet) from least penetrating (α) to most penetrating (γ) radiation.

Later it was discovered that alpha particles were actually helium nuclei, beta particles came in both negative and positive forms and were actually electrons (–) and positrons (+) emitted from the nucleus, and gamma rays were very high-energy photons.

These three nuclear radiations are energetic enough to ionise atoms.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 205
3B

New knowledgeDifferent types of radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Figure 3B–4 shows a gamma ray ionising a helium atom to create a He+He^{+}He+ ion.

NOTE: • Atoms with an overall positive or negative charge are referred to as ions.

Positive ions form when electrons are removed from a neutral atom.

Negative ions form when electrons are gained by a neutral atom.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 206
3B

New knowledgeDifferent types of radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

α-, β- and γ-radiation all have the ability to ionise atoms that they come into contact with.

These three nuclear radiations differ in many important properties; for example, their charge, mass, energy, capacity to penetrate substances, capacity to ionise materials and their behaviour in electric and magnetic fields.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 207
3B

New knowledgeAlpha particle radiation (α)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Alpha particle radiation consists of two neutrons and two protons (that is the same as a helium nucleus) ejected as a package from the nucleus of a radioactive atom.

The package carries two positive charges.

Their charged nature means that they are affected by both electric and magnetic fields.

The speed of the alpha (α) particles depends very much on the nature of the radioactive source, but typically their maximum speed (~30 000 km s−1s^{-1}s−1) is about 10% of the speed of light (Figure 3B–5).

Figure 3B–5 A radioactive nucleus is shown ejecting two protons and two neutrons bound together as a helium nucleus, reducing its mass and becoming a different element. The ejected helium nucleus is called an α-particle, which carries a positive charge. α-particles cannot penetrate a piece of paper or skin but are very dangerous when substances emitting them are ingested or inhaled.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 218
3B

New knowledgeAlpha particle radiation (α)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

The capacity of α-particle radiation to penetrate materials is not very great: it usually penetrates no more than a few centimetres in air and is absorbed even by a relatively small thickness of paper or human skin.

However, because they are travelling so fast, and are relatively massive (compared, say, with β-particles), α-particles can ionise a large number of atoms over their very short range of penetration as they dissipate their kinetic energy.

This makes α-particle radiation relatively harmless for most external sources that are about a metre or more away from us, as the radiation will be easily absorbed by the intervening air.

But if radiation sources are close to or within sensitive organs α-particle radiation is extremely dangerous.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 219
3B

New knowledgeAlpha particle radiation (α)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Alpha particle radiation results in transmutation of elements.

The decaying radioactive nucleus is called the parent nucleus and the produced radionuclide is called the daughter nucleus.

For example, when uranium-238 decays by emitting an α-particle, the original (parent) nucleus is left with four less nucleons (2 protons and 2 neutrons).

The daughter nucleus now has 90 protons, which is the element thorium-234.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2110
3B

New knowledgeAlpha particle radiation (α)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

This can be written as follows: 92238U→90234Th+24He^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}92238​U→90234​Th+24​He + energy Alpha particles are emitted with specific energies that are unique to the properties of the parent nucleus.

In the case of the uranium-238 nucleus, the α-particle emitted has an energy of 4.3 MeV.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2111
3B

New knowledgeUseful applications of alpha radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Although α-particles have low penetrating power, they still provide a range of useful applications: • smoke detectors – americium-241 is commonly used in ionising smoke detectors.

Smoke that enters the detector reduces the amount of α-particles that are detected and triggers the alarm • static eliminators typically use α-particles from polonium-210 to remove static electric charges from equipment • α-emitters are used in radiotherapy to treat cancers • radioisotope thermoelectric generators use α-particle decay from plutonium-238 to generate heat that is converted to electricity; they are commonly used in space probes and robotic planetary explorers (Figure 3B–7).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2312
3B

New knowledgeBeta radiation (β)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Beta particle radiation usually consists of very fast-moving electrons or positrons.

Every beta (β) particle carries either one negative or one positive electronic charge (i.e. ±1.6 × 10−1910^{-19}10−19 coulomb: electron –e, positron +e).

Their charged nature means that they are affected by both electric and magnetic fields (as α-particles are), and this property was also important for their original discovery.

The velocity of β-particles also varies over a wide range, depending on the nature of the radioactive source, but it is usually never more than 90% of the speed of light, c (0.9c or 270 000 km s−1s^{-1}s−1).

Figure 3B–8 Diagram of β⁻-radiation (electrons, left) and β⁺-radiation (positrons, right). The electrons and positrons can move at 90% of the speed of light, c, hence ‘0.9c’. They can penetrate paper or several millimetres of skin. Like α-particles they are harmful when emitted inside the human body.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2413
3B

New knowledgeBeta radiation (β)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Beta particles can penetrate up to 1 metre of air.

They can be absorbed by aluminium a few millimetres thick.

Their ionising capacity is considerably less than that of α-radiation.

However, they penetrate further through materials so they can be dangerous if the source is closer than a metre externally, or very dangerous if the source is ingested internally, for much the same sort of reasons as for α-particle radiation.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2414
3B

New knowledgeBeta radiation (β)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

In β−β^{-}β−-decay an electron is emitted from inside the nucleus.

However, since a nucleus does not contain any electrons, how is this possible?

The electrons emitted do not come from the electron shell surrounding the nucleus.

Some very interesting changes take place inside a radioactive nucleus when it emits an electron.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2415
3B

New knowledgeBeta radiation (β)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

A neutron turns into a proton and emits an electron (β−β^{-}β−).

This can be written as: 01n→11p+−10e^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow {}^{1}_{1}\text{p} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e}01​n→11​p+−10​e + energy or 01n→11p+−10β^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow {}^{1}_{1}\text{p} + {}^{0}_{-1}\beta01​n→11​p+−10​β + energy In a similar manner, a proton can also turn into a neutron, emitting a positron or beta-plus particle (β+β^{+}β+). 11p→01n++10e^{1}_{1}\text{p} \rightarrow {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} + {}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}11​p→01​n++10​e + energy or 11p→01n++10β^{1}_{1}\text{p} \rightarrow {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} + {}^{0}_{+1}\beta11​p→01​n++10​β + energy These β−β^{-}β−- and β+β^{+}β+-emissions are shown in Figure 3B–8.

As noted previously, α-particles are emitted with specific energies that are unique to the parent nucleus.

Beta particles are emitted with any energy up to a maximum value, but not all of the initial energy can be accounted for in the products.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2416
3B

New knowledgeBeta radiation (β)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Does this mean that energy is not conserved in this β-decay nuclear process?

As introduced in Section 3A, Wolfgang Pauli (a theoretical physicist) in 1930 suggested that another particle, as yet undetected, was emitted.

This particle would have no charge, as all the charge was accounted for, and have negligible mass.

Enrico Fermi named the particle ‘neutrino’, from the Italian for ‘little neutral one’.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2417
3B

New knowledgeBeta radiation (β)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

It was first experimentally detected in 1956.

The complete β−β^{-}β−-decay process is: 01n→11p+−10β^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow {}^{1}_{1}\text{p} + {}^{0}_{-1}\beta01​n→11​p+−10​β + neutrino where the neutrino is the carrier of the ‘missing’ energy.

The complete β+β^{+}β+-decay process is: 11p→01n++10β^{1}_{1}\text{p} \rightarrow {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} + {}^{0}_{+1}\beta11​p→01​n++10​β + neutrino where again the neutrino is the carrier of the ‘missing’ energy.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2418
3B

New knowledgeUseful applications of beta radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

The medium penetrating power of β-particles provides a range of useful applications that include: • thickness detectors for the quality control of thin materials, i.e. paper • treatment of eye and bone cancers; strontium-89 is commonly used • fluorine-18 as a tracer for positron emission tomography (PET).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2519
3B

New knowledgeGamma radiation (γ)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Gamma radiation does not consist of charged particles.

It is a form of very short wavelength electromagnetic energy similar to X-ray radiation.

These forms of electromagnetic radiation can be considered as small discrete packages of energy called photons.

The speed of γ-radiation is the speed of light (300 000 km s−1s^{-1}s−1 or c).

Figure 3B–10 X-rays and gamma rays overlap in the electromagnetic spectrum.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2520
3B

New knowledgeGamma radiation (γ)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Gamma radiation is very difficult to stop: even lead that is several centimetres thick does not absorb all of the radiation.

Although the ionising capacity of gamma (γ) rays is considerably smaller than that of β-radiation, their high penetration ability means that they are dangerous even at a distance as they can penetrate our bodies and hit sensitive organs.

This makes γ-radiation extremely dangerous to us, both as an external source and if internally ingested or inhaled.

NOTE: Both γ-rays and X-rays are part of the electromagnetic spectrum and as seen in Figure 3B–10 these two regions of the electromagnetic spectrum overlap.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2521
3B

New knowledgeGamma radiation (γ)

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

X-rays and γ-rays have the same basic properties but originate from different parts of the atom.

X-rays are emitted from processes outside the nucleus, but γ-rays originate inside the nucleus.

X-rays are also generally lower in energy and therefore less penetrating than γ-rays but both have enough energy to ionise atoms.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2522
3B

New knowledgeUseful applications of gamma radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Gamma-emitting radioisotopes are the most widely used radiation sources.

The strong penetrating power of gamma rays has many applications.

The three radioisotopes that are by far the most useful gamma ray emitters are caesium-137, technetium-99m and cobalt-60.

Sterilisation of medical equipment in hospitals; pasteurisation, via irradiation, of certain foodstuffs; levelling or thickness gauges (i.e. food packaging, steel mills); industrial radiography; and medical radiation treatment of cancerous tumours using a gamma ‘knife’ (see Figure 3B–11).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2623
3B

New knowledgeUseful applications of gamma radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Measurement and control of the flow of liquids in industrial processes; investigation of subterranean strata (i.e. oil, coal, gas and other mineralisation); measurement of soil moisture-density at construction sites; and medical radiation treatment of cancerous tumours.

Tc-99m is the most widely used radioactive isotope for medical diagnostic studies in different chemical forms for brain, bone, liver, spleen and kidney imaging.

It is also used for blood flow studies.

Cobalt-60 decays by emitting a low-energy electron (beta particle) from the nucleus and high-energy electromagnetic radiation (gamma rays).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2624
3B

New knowledgeUseful applications of gamma radiation

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

It is an extremely useful radioactive isotope that is used in radiation treatment of cancerous tumours.

It does not exist in nature but can be produced as an artificial radioactive isotope in nuclear reactors.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2625
3B

New knowledgeNuclear transformations

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

A nuclear transformation is the conversion of one nuclide into another.

It can occur by the natural radioactive decay of a nucleus.

For example, carbon-14, a naturally occurring radioactive isotope of carbon, decays via β−β^{-}β−-decay into nitrogen-14 during which one of the neutrons in the carbon atom becomes a proton.

This increases the number of protons in the atom by one, creating a nitrogen atom rather than a carbon atom: 614C→714N+−10β^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\text{N} + {}^{0}_{-1}\beta614​C→714​N+−10​β α-, β- and γ-radiation all change the nucleus in different ways.

Table 3B–1 Nuclear transformation equations involved in α-, β–-, β+- and γ-radioactive decay
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2826
3B

New knowledgeNuclear transformations

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Because both α-radiation and β-radiation are accompanied by changes in the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus, they give rise to the formation of a different element.

Other nuclear transformations can be induced by bombarding elements with other nuclear particles – protons, neutrons, α-particles and so on.

The first artificial nucleus produced by this technique was in Ernest Rutherford’s laboratory in 1917.

Rutherford bombarded nitrogen atoms with high-speed α-particles from a natural radioactive isotope of radium, and observed both protons and an isotope of oxygen resulting from the reaction: 714N+24He→817O+11H^{14}_{7}\text{N} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} \rightarrow {}^{17}_{8}\text{O} + {}^{1}_{1}\text{H}714​N+24​He→817​O+11​H Both the 817O^{17}_{8}\text{O}817​O and 11H^{1}_{1}\text{H}11​H nuclei that are produced are stable.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2827
3B

New knowledgeNuclear transformations

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

The advent of particle accelerators in the early 1930s enabled charged particles such as protons to be fired at atoms.

The advantage of using a particle accelerator is that the energy of the bombarding particle can be accurately controlled.

The limitation of using positively charged particles, however, is that they have to be travelling at very high speed to overcome the electrostatic repulsion of the positively charged nucleus.

In 1932, the physicist James Chadwick bombarded beryllium with α-particles.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2828
3B

New knowledgeNuclear transformations

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

The resulting radiation went through a lead shield, but it was completely unaffected by electric or magnetic fields.

Chadwick had discovered the neutron – a neutral particle with almost the same mass as a proton.

After the neutron was discovered, physicists realised that it would make a good probe for exploring the atomic nucleus as there would be no electrostatic repulsion acting on the neutron.

Nuclear physicists can also use neutrons in breeder nuclear reactors to ‘breed’ fissile plutonium-239 from non-fissile uranium-238.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2829
3B

New knowledgeNuclear transformations

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

This will be important when we look at nuclear reactors and nuclear weapons in Chapter 4.

Alpha particle radiation involves the ejection of two neutrons and two protons (helium nucleus or α-particle) from the nucleus of the radioactive element.

For example, the isotope uranium-238 has 92 protons and 146 neutrons.

In order to achieve greater stability, the nucleus may emit an α-particle, so reducing its number of protons to 90 and its number of neutrons to 144.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2830
3B

New knowledgeNuclear transformations

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

However, it is no longer a uranium nucleus.

Checking the periodic table for Z = 90 indicates it is now an isotope of the element thorium (Th) with atomic number 90 and mass number 234 (90 + 144).

In fact, it is thorium-234.

The decay process can be represented as follows: 92238U→90234Th+24He^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}92238​U→90234​Th+24​He The overall effect of α-particle emission is to produce neutron-rich nuclei; that is, nuclei that have too many neutrons to be stable.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2831
3B

New knowledgeNuclear transformations

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

The nucleus does not simply eject a neutron (or neutrons) to correct this instability.

Instead, one of the neutrons in the nucleus changes into a proton by emitting a β−β^{-}β−-particle; that is, a high-speed electron: 01n→11p+−10e^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow {}^{1}_{1}\text{p} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e}01​n→11​p+−10​e This phenomenon is known as β−β^{-}β−-emission and is an example of the weak nuclear force in action (see Section 3A).

For instance, in the case of thorium-234 (which was formed by the α-particle decay of uranium-238) the nucleus further decays by β−β^{-}β−-emission to protactinium-234 (Pa): 90234Th→91234Pa+−10e^{234}_{90}\text{Th} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{91}\text{Pa} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e}90234​Th→91234​Pa+−10​e In most cases after the emission of an α-particle or a β−β^{-}β−-particle, the nucleus rearranges slightly to minimise its internal energy state.

This rearrangement of the nucleus releases energy in the form of a γ-ray.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2832
3B

New knowledgeNuclear transformations

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

Since γ-ray emission is the emission of energy rather than a particle, it causes no change in either the mass number (A) or the atomic number (Z).

This process occurs almost instantaneously after the α-particle or β−β^{-}β−-particle emission, so γ-rays are emitted along with either an α-particle or a β−β^{-}β−-particle.

For example, sodium-24 decays by emitting a β−β^{-}β−-particle and a γ-ray as follows: 1124Na→1224Mg∗+−10e^{24}_{11}\text{Na} \rightarrow {}^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}^{*} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e}1124​Na→1224​Mg∗+−10​e 1224Mg∗→1224Mg+00γ^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}^{*} \rightarrow {}^{24}_{12}\text{Mg} + {}^{0}_{0}\gamma1224​Mg∗→1224​Mg+00​γ The asterisk (*) signifies that the nucleus is excited (i.e. unstable) and has excessive internal energy.

Eventually sodium-24 decays to stable magnesium-24.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 2833

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation
An α-particle emitted from a radioactive element has an energy of 2.99 × 10−1210^{-12}10−12 J.
How much energy does this represent in electronvolts (eV)?

Working

The conversion factor between eV and joule is:
1 eV = 1.6 × 10−1910^{-19}10−19 J
Therefore, the energy of the α-particle can be written as:
2.99×10−121.6×10−19\frac{2.99 \times 10^{-12}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}1.6×10−192.99×10−12​ = 1.87 × 10710^{7}107 eV
= 18.7 MeV
1.87 × 10710^{7}107 eV = 18.7 MeV

Working

EK=12×6.64×10−27×(2×107)2E_K = \frac{1}{2} \times 6.64 \times 10^{-27} \times (2 \times 10^{7})^{2}EK​=21​×6.64×10−27×(2×107)2
= 1.33 × 10−1210^{-12}10−12 J (2 marks)

You tryWorksheet 3B–1 Alpha, beta and gamma radiation Q3b

Alpha, beta and gamma radiation
An α-particle emitted from a particular radioactive element is travelling at 20 000 km s−1s^{-1}s−1. The mass of an α-particle is 6.64 × 10−2710^{-27}10−27 kg.
How much energy does this represent in electronvolts (eV) for the α-particle?

Working

The conversion factor between electronvolts and joules is:
1 eV = 1.6 × 10−1910^{-19}10−19 J
Therefore, the energy of the α-particle can be written as:
1.33×10−121.6×10−19\frac{1.33 \times 10^{-12}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}1.6×10−191.33×10−12​ = 8.3 × 10610^{6}106 eV = 8.3 MeV (2 marks)
